messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Raj, a 58-year-old product manager, had long carried the weight of a traumatic past that had transformed his vibrant life into a landscape of fear and isolation. Growing up in South Asia, he had once been full of hope and ambition. However, everything changed during a harrowing event in his late twenties when he was captured and tortured by political extremists. The pain of that experience haunted him, not just as a memory but as a living presence that reshaped his perceptions and interactions. The sound of incomprehensible chatter, reminiscent of the voices he heard during his captivity, sent waves of dizziness through him, leaving him feeling lightheaded and disoriented, as if he were being pulled back into that terrible place.

Months turned into years, and Raj found himself withdrawing from life as he became increasingly convinced that nothing good could happen to him anymore. This belief turned into a lens through which he viewed the world, fostering a deep mistrust of those around him. Having come to believe that he was perpetually in danger and that his vulnerability made him a target, Raj felt that the only sensible response was to withdraw from relationships and avoid any social situations that might expose him to further harm. As he navigated his daily life, he avoided anything that could be stressful, from high-pressure meetings at work to social gatherings with friends. Raj had come to believe that the world was a dangerous place, and with that belief, staying home felt like the only rational strategy to keep himself safe from potential threats. Each day, he would wake up in a state of heightened alert, his body tensed, and his mind racing with thoughts of potential dangers that lurked just beyond his perception. With the world feeling so threatening, Raj found himself devising strategies to minimize his exposure, leading him to avoid even the simplest errands or gatherings, as he believed that staying home was the only way to truly keep himself safe. Even in the safety of his home, he could not relax. The panic would grip him, forcing him to check the locks on the doors multiple times before he could settle into bed.

Raj’s coping mechanisms became intertwined with his beliefs, creating a vicious cycle that was hard to escape. His constant body monitoring led him to believe there was something intrinsically wrong with him, a fault that made him susceptible to danger, further reinforcing his negative appraisals. Each time Raj resorted to checking the locks on his doors multiple times before bed, he felt it served as proof of his inability to cope, deepening his conviction that he was more fragile than others. He began to perceive the world through a lens of danger, where every unexpected touch from his wife would cause him to startle, as if the gentle gesture was a threat. Each jolt left him more convinced of his frailty and inability to cope. He avoided any reminders of his trauma, particularly anything that might resemble military uniforms or even the sight of weapons, fearing that such triggers would unleash a wave of memories he wasn't prepared to face. His withdrawal from the world had turned into a self-fulfilling prophecy; every missed opportunity to confront these reminders only strengthened the grip of his trauma, making them more tangible and frightening. His avoidance strategies created a ripple effect, as each choice to sidestep a potential reminder of his trauma solidified his triggers, turning everyday sights and sounds into reminders of the past he sought to escape. Each event he chose to avoid became a marker of his trauma, reinforcing the belief that he was unable to face the world, and this growing list of avoided situations only confirmed to him that he was indeed inescapably broken.

As he navigated his role as a product manager, Raj found himself increasingly isolated. Meetings were fraught with tension; he would sit silently, paralyzed by his anxiety, while the sounds of sirens from the street would send him into a tailspin of panic. He feared he might lose control, that he might reveal the extent of his suffering if anyone noticed his distress. The laughter of his colleagues, the easy banter exchanged in the break room, felt like a different world—a world he could not be a part of. In his mind, he believed that reaching out for help would only expose his perceived weakness, confirming his belief that he could not trust others.

After years of enduring this self-imposed exile, Raj finally felt the weight of his burden becoming unbearable. A recent incident at a family gathering, where a loud noise had caused him to flee to the bathroom trembling, shattered any remaining illusion of control. It was a stark reminder that he could no longer manage his symptoms alone. He realized that the life he had built, filled with avoidance and anxiety, had begun to take a toll on his marriage and his sense of self. His wife, deeply concerned and confused, had urged him to seek help, prompting Raj to confront the reality of his situation.

As he sat in the waiting room of the therapist’s office, he felt a mixture of fear and hope. What frightened him most was the possibility that confronting his past would deepen his wounds rather than heal them. Yet, as he waited, he couldn’t shake the thought that perhaps this time, with help, he might reclaim the life that had been stolen from him—one where he could trust others and find peace within himself.

violation_explanations: The vignette does not clearly establish that negative appraisals lead to maladaptive strategies.
The vignette lacks a clear connection showing that perceived threat leads to the use of maladaptive strategies.
The vignette does not convey that maladaptive strategies reinforce negative appraisals.
The vignette does not illustrate how maladaptive strategies lead to triggers being reinforced.
